title: How Hosting Works
subtitle: From code on your laptop to users around the world — the complete hosting stack explained

content.text: What actually happens when someone visits your site

When a user types myapp.com in their browser, a remarkable chain of events happens in milliseconds: a DNS lookup translates the domain to an IP address, a TCP connection is established, a TLS handshake encrypts the channel, an HTTP request is sent, a server processes it, and a response is returned. Hosting is the art of making that chain work reliably, quickly, and securely for all your users simultaneously.

content.code:
User types: https://myapp.com/dashboard

1. DNS Resolution (0-50ms)
   Browser → DNS server
   'What IP is myapp.com?'
   DNS → '203.0.113.42'

2. TCP Connection (10-100ms depending on distance)
   Browser → 203.0.113.42:443
   Three-way handshake: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK

3. TLS Handshake (10-50ms)
   Client: 'I support TLS 1.3, here are my cipher preferences'
   Server: 'Here's my certificate, let's use this cipher'
   Both: derive shared encryption keys
   All further communication is encrypted

4. HTTP Request (sent over encrypted connection)
   GET /dashboard HTTP/2
   Host: myapp.com
   Cookie: session=abc123

5. Server Processing (1ms - 2000ms)
   Web server (Nginx) receives request
   Routes to application (Node.js, Python, etc.)
   Application runs business logic, queries database
   Returns response

6. HTTP Response
   200 OK
   Content-Type: text/html
   <html>...</html>

7. Browser renders the HTML, loads CSS/JS/images (parallel requests)

STATIC HOSTING (HTML/CSS/JS files only)
  What: Files served directly from a file server or CDN
  Examples: GitHub Pages, Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages, S3
  Runs: React, Vue, Svelte (built), plain HTML sites, docs
  Cost: Free to ~$20/month
  Scaling: Automatic (CDN edge nodes handle any traffic)
  Ops: Near zero — just deploy files

SERVERLESS (functions)
  What: Code runs on-demand per request, no persistent server
  Examples: Vercel Edge Functions, AWS Lambda, Cloudflare Workers
  Runs: API endpoints, server-side rendering, webhooks
  Cost: Pay per request (usually very cheap, first 1M free)
  Scaling: Instant (platform handles everything)
  Ops: Near zero — upload code, it runs

CONTAINER PLATFORMS (managed)
  What: Your Docker container runs on managed infrastructure
  Examples: Railway, Render, Fly.io, AWS ECS Fargate
  Runs: Any containerized app — Node.js APIs, Python, Go
  Cost: $5-50/month for small apps
  Scaling: Auto-scaling available
  Ops: Low — deploy containers, platform manages servers

VPS / DEDICATED SERVER
  What: You get a Linux VM, full control
  Examples: DigitalOcean, Linode, Hetzner, AWS EC2
  Runs: Anything
  Cost: $5-200/month depending on size
  Scaling: Manual (you provision more servers)
  Ops: High — you manage OS, web server, updates, monitoring

Rule: match hosting type to your app's needs
Start simple (static or serverless), add complexity only as needed

content.text: Static vs dynamic — understanding your stack

content.code:
STATIC SITE:
  Every user gets the same files
  Content generated at BUILD TIME (not request time)
  No server-side computation per request
  Examples: marketing site, docs, blog
  Frameworks: Plain HTML, Astro, Next.js SSG, Gatsby, Hugo

DYNAMIC APP:
  Content varies per user/request
  Generated at REQUEST TIME based on user data
  Requires a running server
  Examples: dashboard showing user data, social feed, e-commerce checkout
  Requires: Node.js/Python/Go server + database

SPA (Single Page Application) — a hybrid:
  App shell is STATIC (same HTML/JS for everyone)
  But data is DYNAMIC (fetched from API after load)
  React/Vue/Svelte apps are usually SPAs
  → Host the static files on CDN (free, fast)
  → Host the API separately (Node.js server)
  → Best of both worlds

SSR (Server-Side Rendering):
  HTML is generated on server per request (like PHP)
  Good for SEO (HTML is ready for crawlers)
  Next.js / Nuxt.js support SSR
  → Requires a running server (can't use pure static hosting)

content.text: Your architecture decision determines your hosting options. A pure React SPA (Vite build) can be hosted on GitHub Pages for free — no server needed. If you add Next.js SSR, you need a platform that runs Node.js. If you add a PostgreSQL database, you need a separate database host. Make conscious choices about which features require which infrastructure.

questions.question: You built a React app that shows a public list of products (same for all users) fetched from an API. Can you host the frontend on a static host like GitHub Pages?
options: No — React apps require a Node.js server
Yes — the React app itself is a static set of files (HTML/JS/CSS). It fetches the product data from your API after loading in the browser
Only if the products don't change often
Yes, but only if you use Next.js
questions.explanation: A React SPA is just files: index.html, app.js, app.css. The browser downloads these static files, runs the JavaScript, and the JavaScript then fetches data from your API. The frontend has no idea what server it runs from — it works identically whether served from GitHub Pages, Vercel, or any CDN. Only your API server needs dynamic hosting. This is the SPA model: static shell + dynamic API.

faq.q: What's the difference between a web server (Nginx) and an application server (Node.js)?
faq.a: A web server (Nginx, Apache) handles HTTP protocol, serves static files, terminates SSL, and proxies requests to application servers. An application server (Node.js, Gunicorn, etc.) runs your actual code and generates dynamic responses. In production, they're typically layered: Nginx listens on port 80/443, handles SSL, then forwards dynamic requests to Node.js on port 3000. Nginx is very efficient at static files and network handling; Node.js is where your business logic lives.

examples: Stack Overflow's main site famously handles 500M page views per month with just 11 web servers and 4 SQL servers — because they serve mostly static content, use aggressive caching, and have highly optimized database queries. Most traffic is served from RAM cache, never hitting the database
Hacker News runs on a single server (arc4.ycombinator.com) with about 7 million monthly visitors. Simple architecture + good caching beats complex infrastructure for most use cases
